utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Galeva, do you remember that the Prosecutor, on cross-examination, put several questions to you about the takeover competencies of the Ljuboten case on the part of this Tribunal? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In transcript, this is 8840 and 8841.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You answered several questions, and you confirmed that you were aware of the fact that the Prosecutor had asked and was permitted a transfer of the case into his competence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a lawyer, and as an employee of the Ministry of Interior, were you aware of the fact that the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal at any given moment could have asked for this case to be transferred from authority of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware that that was the regular proper procedure and that such a possibility was provided for.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal applied to the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal to defer that case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that took place sometime in September of 2002, when the case was deferred to the competence of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, were you aware of the fact that some measures or some information had been undertaken by the Prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia with regard to that application on the part of The Hague Tribunal Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I am aware that before the case was transferred from Macedonia to the Tribunal, before it was deferred to the competence of the Tribunal, the public prosecutor general of Macedonia had some meetings; and, of course, there was written correspondence, applications sent to the Tribunal, by which he requested that he be informed in writing about everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 1D75, page 4 in the Macedonian version, bullet point 4. And in the English version, it is page 5, bullet point 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, you will have the same text in the Macedonian language before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please blow up on bullet point 4. This is it. On page 5 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I'm going to read to you bullet point 4, which reads as follows: "The public prosecutor of the Republic of Macedonia was not informed by any letter or decision of The Hague Tribunal that the Macedonian authorities should cease all further investigations in relation to these cases; and, as a result of that, in the Republic of Macedonia, in accordance with the constitution, the Law on Criminal Procedure, the criminal code and other laws, acts have been undertaken by the competent organs. These acts been undertaken in relation to the known and unknown perpetrators, which are revealed additionally during the proceedings."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the following page to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I would kindly ask you, Mrs. Galeva, to listen to bullet point 2, which reads as follows: "Meetings were held in order to help the OTP i.e., the Prosecutor's office of The Hague Tribunal, in relation to the pending obstacles which they had in relation to the investigation they conduct and adequate result have been achieved after those meetings." Mrs. Galeva, in the year 2002, when you worked in Mr. Boskoski's office, were you familiar with this position of the Macedonian prosecutor who insisted on proceeding with investigations and who, at the same time, closely cooperated with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware. I had heard about it in several meetings and collegiums where I was present that the public prosecutor general expected formal application to be submitted to him with regards to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The prosecutor also asked you whether the interest of Mr. Boskoski was in protecting the national interest of the Macedonian people and the Macedonian police's reputation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 8808.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you remember that the prosecutor asked you about that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you stated that Mr. Boskoski showed a particular interest in establishing the real truth about the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said it already several times during my previous statements that he was particularly interested in learning the real truth about the Ljuboten case as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering the Prosecutor's questions, you tried to clarify and explain, if I may paraphrase, that it was in the best interests of Mr. Boskoski to establish the real truth; and if it is established that there are people who are responsible, including himself, that this should be clarified; and if this was not the case, that all talks should talk with that. Did I understand your answer to the Prosecutor well? Is that the gist of your answer to the Prosecutor's questions?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember my answer, and I remain at the statement that the position of the minister was clear, the position of Mr. Ljube Boskoski, that it is necessary to investigate the truth about this case as soon as possible and to establish any involvement of -- on the part of police officers or any individuals maybe in the events, as there was speculations and rumours in the public, and if anything of the sort were established. But not only on the basis of rumours but corroborated by facts, by arguments, of course those persons should be held responsible and criminal or misdemeanour reports to be submitted against them or that the person should be disciplined within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, the position that you have just repeated with regard to Minister Boskoski's position, did that position have any impact on the reputation of the police?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there was an impact on the reputation of the police and that was one of the major efforts of Mr. Ljube Boskoski as the leader of the police. Of course, the reputation of the police and of the Ministry of Interior was very important for him, and this is why he wanted to establish the truth, because it had a strong impact on the reputation of the police and it was necessary to establish as soon as possible whether that was truth or not. And if there were such people, then those people should have been sanctioned and removed from the ministry. So he persistently made efforts to find such participants, if any, because it had an impact on the reputation of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will remember, Mrs. Galeva, the Prosecutor asked you several questions, suggesting to you that Minister Boskoski had a negative attitude to the Human Rights Watch and the Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 8837 and 8838.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, that the Prosecutor asked you that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you did provide a certain answer to the -- that kind of questions, can you please repeat: Were you familiar with the minister's position to the non-governmental organisations and toward this is Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what I had heard during my presence in the meetings and attendance in the collegiums, and such collegiums were convened by Mr. Ljube Boskoski as the then minister. He publicly presented his position regarding the Tribunal, in the sense that we need to work to cooperate and to support the Tribunal and that we should make available all relevant information related to the event, to the Tribunal. With regards to other international and other non-governmental organisations, there were many, I can't really distinguish between individual cases and give you the names of those, but can I tell you that there was -- that he thought that it was not proper to present misinformation to the public, if I may say so, because whatever information were presented, they were presented offhand. They were uncorroborated. They were unsubstantiated. Those were rumours only.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the witness to be shown P548, Exhibit number P548, please, page 2 of the document. This is a public announcement by the Ministry of Interior. I'm interested in the last paragraph on page 1 and the beginning of the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I'm going to read to you one part of this announcement by the Ministry of Interior, which says as follows: "By conducting the exhumation with autopsy, the identity of the five corpses and the cause of their death shall be determined, which shall contribute towards eliminating all speculations which specific representatives of the Human Rights Watch tried to present to the public against the Ministry of Interior and OSCE, that the five persons of Albanian ethnicity from village of Ljuboten are unnecessary victims of the Macedonian security forces because allegedly they were not members of the armed terrorist groups of the so-called ONA." Mrs. Galeva, tell me, please, this way of expression that I've just read out to you from the public announcement about some individuals in the Human Rights Watch organisation, is it something that you could hear from the minister when he was saying that some individuals are presenting things that are unsubstantiated and that those things have to be verified?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I clarified that already, what was the intention of the minister in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 1D202. The page is 1D6045. In the English version, it is 6044. Actually, it is the other way around. In the Macedonian, it is 1D6044; and in the English version, the page number is 1D6045. This is a transcript of a public statement issued by Mr. Boskoski. The document number is 1D202.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph from the bottom in the Macedonian version, it says as follows: "Ljube Boskoski: We respect the international Tribunal, and we will do everything necessary to submit the crimes that occurred in the Republic of Macedonia; and to this end, we have submitted evidence. You know that the criminal reports were submitted against approximately 20 individuals for serious crimes, crimes which are persecuted in accordance with the international law, crimes which are within the jurisdiction of The Hague Tribunal; so, of course, we will cooperate." Would this also confirm what was the position of Mr. Boskoski towards the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the witness to be shown Exhibit number P402; page 99 in the Macedonian version and page N000-9704-ET-02 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I apologise for my bad pronunciation of the Macedonian language, but I believe that all the time you have the text in front of you and that you can follow.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 -- first, let me tell you that this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. It's the Prosecution's recollection that, during cross-examination, the Prosecution asked the witness about her -- her particular perception of the organisation known as Human Rights Watch. It may have asked the witness - I simple can't recall right now - whether Mr. Boskoski made any comments about Human Rights Watch. It certainly did not ask any general or broader questions about the feelings or level of cooperation or not of Mr. Boskoski with the entire international community, nor do I believe this Tribunal. So I think we're going really beyond the scope of cross-examination here, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that my learned friend's objection is correct because there was no reference or direct reference to the international Tribunal, but several questions were put to the witness about the international Tribunal in the sense that this case was opened only to be referred to the Tribunal, and that before that, there were no efforts whatsoever to submit the materials to the Tribunal. And in that sense, an attempt has been made to say that Mrs. Galeva's work and tasks were, in that sense, an indication of Mr. Boskoski's attitude towards the Tribunal; and, especially, Mr. Saxon said, on page 8811, he asked the witness: "Mrs. Galeva what did Mr. Boskoski tell you about this Tribunal?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, now you have before you the text that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see the following page, page 99, please. Maybe it has been downloaded differently so the following page cannot seen. Now we have it, yes. This is exactly what I need, and I would kindly ask you to do the same in the English version. Can we see the next page in the English version as well, so that the two pages actually correspond in their contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 on the page that you have before you, it says as follows: "On one occasion, I was thanked for the good collaboration and the abundant material we had delivered to The Hague Tribunal. "My interlocutor emphasised that he knew Macedonia was going through very difficult times and that The Hague Tribunal had not opened any proceedings at all. But, in terms of human rights violations, he added, one of the ambiguous cases was Ljuboten and that case would need to be investigated. "I replied that the Macedonian authorities stood at the Tribunal's disposal and would provide all the facts available to help clarify this case, which certain individuals were exploiting with the aim of having me directly indicted." This position presented in the book, "My Fight for Macedonia," does it also confirm what you have just testified about as to what you could hear from Mr. Boskoski as his end position towards the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, this is one of the proofs for his efforts, as well as the cooperation with the ICTY, to discover everything related to the Ljuboten case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about your conversation with Judge Nikolovski. Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember that both on examination-in-chief and later on, you stated that the judge told you, on that occasion, that all the cases had to be referred to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to call for Exhibit P55.18 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, you have before you a document issued by the Basic Court Skopje II, which was signed by Investigative Judge Dragan Nikolovski. You can see his signature there. Is that the same judge that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read the text to you; it is not long. This letter was sent to Mr. Lopez-Terres, and it says: "Dear Mr. Lopez-Terres, I have so far asked on two occasions by fax that you confirm in writing that, after the conducted analysis, the expert examination of the material seized by the Tribunal, this entire material will be delivered to me along with the results of the analysis. "In view of the fact that you only confirmed that I will be given the analysis results and it was not explicitly confirmed that the material will be delivered to me, I ask that you do so by fax or that you enable me, as investigative judge, to be present during the analysis of the material which is to be conducted at the Netherlands Forensic Institute in Rijswijk. "Due to the fact that in accordance with the provisions of our code of criminal procedure, the investigative judge determines the expert examination (the analysis) with a written order. He is present at the expert examination and directs the expert examination. "Taking into account that you greed that all expenses arising from such analysis will be borne by The Hague Tribunal, I ask that you confirm that my expenses regarding my stay in the Netherlands will be covered, as well as the expenses in relation to obtaining a Dutch Visa and the travelling expenses. "Should I be granted this, I need to be duly notified of the date when the expert examination is scheduled." Do you remember, Mrs. Galeva, that in your conversation with Judge Nikolovski, he mentioned this request of his which was based on the laws and regulations of the Republic of Macedonia and that he sent to The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I remember that conversation. It was said that even during the procedure of exhumation and autopsy, Mr. Tucker, in a way, made a promise that he will send parts of the report of the analysis, as well as the materials taken for this expert forensic examination. If direct presence of our investigating judge or judges during the procedure in the institute in the Netherlands is impossible. Since that was not done, then, of course, the investigating judge, Mr. Dragan Nikolovski, submitted a written motion to have the materials received or to receive the report that he hadn't received despite that promise made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like the witness to be shown 1D201. This is a letter which Judge Nikolovski received in reply from Mr. Lopez, the head of investigations. I'm going to read on page 1, starting with paragraph 3 in the Macedonian version, which reads: "In view of the decision of Madam Del Ponte to exercise the primacy of the Tribunal in these matters, it is anticipated that all further investigations into these five matters will cease. "However, that will not include current inquiries that are in progress in relation to these investigations (for example, in respect of the Ljuboten investigation, the forensic analysis and subsequent reports, the autopsy reports on the identity of the deceased, and the cause of death, et cetera). "Finally, I refer to your request concerning the return of the ballistic material, subject of the same Ljuboten investigation, to the Skopje II Court. In consequence of Madam Prosecutor's decision, all the ballistic material will be retained by the ICTY until this office ends its investigations."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 2, both in the Macedonian and the English versions. I will continue reading in the meantime: "The ballistic material will be forwarded to the Forensic Institute, Rijswijk, Netherlands, for analysis as planned. During the analysis of this material, no member of this institution will be present. Under the circumstances, there is no necessity for your presence during the process."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your conversation with Mr. Nikolovski, the investigating judge, were you informed, Mrs. Galeva, that the judge was not allowed to continue participating in the proceedings as is envisaged under the law of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The judge also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Prosecutor

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- the Prosecutor also asked you questions about Ljube Krstevski. The question was whether you asked from the minister to order Krstevski to cooperate with you and whether he -- you also asked the minister for Goran Mitevski to cooperate with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been reported on pages 8819 and 8821.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that I was asked that question, and you already have my reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were employed in Minister Boskoski's office, did you ever hear the minister issue orders to the heads of departments in the Ministry of Interior -- in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all. The procedure in the Ministry of Interior was to work on the basis of collegium convened by the minister, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, and that collegium could be held in a broader or more narrow basis depending on the cases processed or the facts discussed, which means that the hierarchical structure was strictly followed, line of hierarchy that exists in the ministry. And in no way, was he able to circumvent the directors as his direct subordinates. He was only able to issue instructions to the directors, and then the directors organised their work within their sphere; and they would then delegate to the heads as the hierarchy follows. They would issue instructions to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Galeva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. Mrs. Galeva, may I thank you. The questioning of you has now concluded. Your presence here in The Hague and the assistance you have been able to give to the Chamber is appreciated. You will now, of course, be able to return to Macedonia, and the court officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber understands that there is a procedural matter which I think you wish to raise, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honour, and we're grateful for the time. On the 25th of January of this year, Your Honour will recall that we filed a motion pursuant to Rule 66(B) and Rule 54, whereby we had are sought to obtain an order from the Chamber for the Prosecution to disclose a number of documents, or rather, categories of documents which the Defence believed came within the terms of Rule 66(B). On Thursday last week, the Chamber rejected the Defence application on basis that the Defence had failed to establish the materiality of the categories of materials sought as requested by the Rules. Today, the Defence would wish to renew its application pursuant to Rule 54 and 66(B). However, in relation to a separate category of material, or at least a category of material, Your Honour, which we submit should permit the Chamber to grant the order sought. Today, the Defence is seeking a similar order pursuant to the same rule in relation, however, to a narrower group of documents; namely, a document or a list, group of documents which have been identified by the Office of the Prosecutor, collected by the Office of the Prosecutor, and kept by the Office of the Prosecutor as going to the credit, the Prosecution says, of the Defence witnesses. Before embarking on the submissions in relation to this application, Your Honour, we would simply first like to refer to a decision of this Trial Chamber of the 13th of September of 2007. It was an oral decision of Your Honours, and I will briefly remind you it related to the record of a meeting between the Prosecutor of this Tribunal and a number of state officials of the government of Macedonia, including Mr. Boskoski. At the time, the Defence will made an application to have access this document. And Mr. Saxon had taken the position on behalf of the Prosecutor that, having reviewed the material, he taken the view that the material was not of the sort that would fall between the rules of procedure and, therefore, did not need to be disclosed. And the Chamber, on that basis, decided that the material did not need to be disclosed. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Mettraux, is this a motion on notice to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. We have sent a notification, I believe, on Thursday or Friday morning, I apologise, and, again, yesterday, to the effect that we would renew the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, Your Honour, it depends on what you mean by notice. We saw -- there was an e-mail that was cc'd to the Prosecutor. I can't recite it by heart, but we were informed that an application would be made. First, we were informed it would be related to 66(A)(ii) and 66(B). Then last evening, I believe, there was a second e-mail, informing the Chamber's legal officer that the Defence wished to make an application pursuant to Rule 66(B). That was the length and breath and depth of the notice provided to the Prosecution; nothing about the content of the motion or what it pertained specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Your Honour, if we can clarify this matter, the only issue which we have raised with the Prosecution in relation to 66(B) to that point in exchange of letter relates to the very material which we are now seeking to obtain pursuant to that Rule. Concerning Rule 66(A)(ii), as Mr. Saxon indicated, our original e-mail referred to that Rule as well. In the meantime, the Prosecution has provided us a letter which responded to that particular aspect of our inquiry; namely, whether there were any the statements of witnesses of the Prosecutor which were outstanding. Mr. Saxon, very properly over the weekend, disclosed to the Defence one particular record of interview of one particular Prosecution witness who had not previously been disclosed to the Defence, and Mr. Saxon also indicated in this letter that, to his knowledge, there were no other statement or records of interview pertaining to any witness that needed to be disclosed. On that basis, there was no need, and there is no need, for us today to make any application pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). As far as the application made pursuant to Rule 66(B), Your Honour, we have, as I indicated, mentioned it twice to the Prosecution that we would make that application, and the only exchange of letter which we ever had with the Prosecution in relation to this matter relates to the very material for which the application is now being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you again, please, for me, summarize or identify the material that is the subject of this present application.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence, originally, I believe, on the 24th of January of this year, made a request to the Prosecution which was relevantly brought in scope to obtain material which the Prosecution had collected and received in the course of additional or further investigation which they had carried out notably since the time of the end of the Prosecution case. We had identified particular documents and types of material, and Mr. Saxon complied with all of our requests but for a particular type of material, where Mr. Saxon indicated to the Defence that the Prosecution would not disclose to the Defence certain documents which had now come in their possession and which related to the credit, the Prosecution says, of our witnesses based, again the Prosecution says, on a decision of this Chamber of, I believe, the 12th of April of last year, which related to the notification of intent to use certain material. So, perhaps to summarize, Your Honour, the material which we are now being denied is material that has been identified by the Prosecution as being relevant to the credit of our witness and, we say, material to the preparation of our case. The reasoning of the Prosecution - and I will be corrected by Mr. Saxon, but this position has been reiterated in several letters to the Defence - is to the effect that the original decision of Your Honours of the 12th of April of 2007 was to the effect that the party would be under no duty to disclose to the other side material that would go to the credit of a particular witness. We understand Your Honours' ruling in quite a different way, in the sense that it did not, in any way, narrow down the disclosure obligation of the Prosecution in particular, but permitted or provided an exception to the duty that was otherwise placed on the party to notify the other side of the material which they intend to use. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue arrises are you not, in truth, merely, seeking to reargue that which has been the subject of our very recent decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what we believe is the case is, and what we would seek from the Chamber, is to do what the Chamber did in relation to the application which we had originally made in relation to the record of this particular meeting, which is simply to rely on the Prosecution own assessment of the materiality of the material which they have in their possession, to find, in effect, that this material being relevant to the credit of the witnesses must be disclosed pursuant to Rule 662. We submit, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is your answer yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Our answer, Your Honour, would be in part; the "in part" being that we believe that we have now made an effort to narrow down the material, which should permit the Chamber to make the order and to come within the term of Rule 66(B)(ii). The Defence is in no position, Your Honour, to identify that material other than relying on the statement made by Mr. Saxon, to the effect that he possessed such material. We do submit that Rule 66(B)(ii) should provide in those circumstances for a way for the Defence to obtain that material with a view to A, we submit, decide whether or not to call a witness; if indeed the Prosecution has in its possession material which would show that a witness is, indeed, not credible or otherwise not reliable, we submit that the disclosure of that material would permit the Defence to make an informed decision as to whether to call a particular witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if could you pause there for a moment, please, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has difficulty, Mr. Mettraux, in seeing that it would be appropriate to allow you to what we see to be reopen what has been decided. You're dealing with some of the same subject matter. You now want to package it a little differently and put it forward specifically; but it, in the Chamber's view, is, in truth, to reargue what has been decided and dealt. So I am afraid we cannot hear you further.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness is one you would be leading, Ms. Residovic? Before the witness is called, the Chamber is interested in timing today. If the witness came in now, it would only be for a relatively short time, and then we would have the first break. We understand from a memorandum received from you that have you a concern later this week that there should be some change in the normal format because of the needs of the next witness. It concerns the Chamber that there -- it could be worth experimenting this week with our format of listings and the times that we have breaks. And I'm just very quickly trying to see the consequences of us breaking now, rather than in a short time after this witness commences. I think it would make little different today, and it may be of some advantage for the rest of the week if we look toward finishing just a little earlier each evening; and to that end, had our first break now, then resumed and had two full sessions with this witness. We will then see tomorrow and Wednesday whether an earlier finish has any significant effect on our progress. I think it may not, given the present witness and the witness to come. So would it be convenient to you to have our first break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that this is very convenient for us. Thank you very much. Our memorandum, as you are aware, was related to another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 20 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojkov. We have already met before, but nevertheless I will introduce the Defence team of Mr. Boskoski. I'm Edina Residovic, and together with Mr. Mettraux, I appear for Mr. Boskoski before this Trial Chamber. Before I start putting questions to you, I would first kindly ask you to state your name and family name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Igno Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, I will kindly ask you this: When you hear my question, please wait for the question to be interpreted and only then start giving your answer. This is it very important because you probably understand me as well as I you, but my question and your answers have to be also heard and understood by the Trial Chamber and by my learned friends in the courtroom. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me where and when were you born, Mr. Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: 29th April 1968, in Kavadarci in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: High school education.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where and when did you graduate from high school?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Economic secondary school in Skopje, and I'm now finishing my studies at the faculty of forestry.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, when did you start working? When were you first employed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In 1991, at the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, your professional life started with the Ministry of Interior. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. My first employment was at the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, today, where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I'm still at the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly give us an overview of the jobs that you have held at the Ministry of Interior since 1991.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Upon my employment in 1991 at the ministry, for a certain period of time, I was an apprentice; then, in 1992, I completed my apprenticeship; and until 1995, I was an operative at the unit for special tasks. In 1995 until 1998, I was junior inspector at the special task unit; then from 1998 till 2000, inspector, head in the sector of operative reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, working as an independent inspector with the internal affairs department in Gazi Baba, were you only involved in the white-collar crimes and crimes against property or were you also involved in other cases?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In 2000, I was transferred in June as inspector for property crimes. But in the police station, or, that is to say, in the unit for internal affairs in Gazi Baba, since there was only one inspector on homicide, in some cases I was also engaged or I was assisting in cases of homicide.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have given us an overview of your jobs and tasks up to 2001. After that, did you have any other jobs; and if you did, could you please tell us briefly what jobs those were?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In September 2001, I was assigned as assistance to the working group for documenting the events and war crimes committed on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia during the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in those jobs; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I believe it was until the beginning of 2003. Afterwards, I came back to work as inspector on motor vehicles in the unit of internal affairs in Avtokomanda. And in 2003, I sent an application to be transferred to the unit for illicit trade of drugs and arms where I was redeployed in December 2003.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Stojkov, what is your job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As of 2003, to the 1st of August of this year -- or rather, 2007, I was independent inspector at the unit for illicit drugs and arms trafficking at the sector for illicit drug and arms trade. And as of the 1st of August, 2007, up until now, I'm independent inspector, head of an operative group at the special mobile police unit for fight against crime.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The unit that you are currently affiliated with, how long has it existed within the Ministry of Interior; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I believe this unit was set up sometime in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkov. You have given us a lot of detail of the jobs that you have held at the Ministry of Interior. In the course of your employment, have you had any special trainings or did you attend any courses in order to be able to perform the duties that you were charged with?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. In 1999, I took part in a training seminar organised by the federal German police forces for following and dealing in cases with illicit drug trafficking. In 2000, I also attended a training seminar organised by the British police for international control and transport of arms and drugs and narcotics. In 2004, I was called by the American Secret Service on a training seminar dealing with weapons of mass destruction. And in 2005, the American Radiology Institute invited me to take part in a training seminar for radioactive weapons. In 2006, we had a joint seminar with the French unit for fight against narcotics. And in 2007, in Cairo, I stayed a longer while for a training in a training seminar against global terrorism organised by the Egyptian police forces, and I believe it was Europol.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have just told us, you have underwent permanent police training all this time. Tell me, Mr. Stojkov, why is it important that you as a policeman undergo certain training and exercises of this kind?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: With gaining its independence and the formation of the Macedonian police, it was very important at the onset to start with the reforms of the police and to have further training of people who were employed there. We knew -- or rather, later, as an employee, I was involved in certain activities, and I knew that Macedonia was part of the transitional countries on the Balkan drug route and other illicit activities, so many of my colleagues and I were included in these police reforms, or rather, further training and specialisation seminars from other countries.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, just one more question concerning your professional background and your capability to perform the policing work. As a worker and as an employee of the Ministry of Interior, have you ever received any awards? Has your work of been recognised or criticised matter?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I already said, I'm an employee of the ministry as of 1991, from the very onset of the Macedonian police; that is to say, I am 16 years now an active police officer. Up until now I have never been reprimanded in any kind. I have been often acknowledged and I have received awards, as one can see from my professional dossier.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will base my questions on documents; therefore, I would kindly ask the usher to provide the Trial Chamber, the witness, and my learned friends from the Prosecution with my binder of documents that I will be using during my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, when you described your assignments in the Ministry of Interior, I noticed that since, or rather, from September 2001 up until the beginning of 2003, you were a member of the working gorup for documenting war crimes. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how you were assigned to this work?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In September 2001, after the conflict, we had some days of rest and I used these free days. When we came back to work, we had a working meeting. I was still at the police station, or rather, the unit in Gazi Baba as inspector for motor vehicles. When I came to this meeting, one of my colleagues, who, during my absence, was assigned to assist the working group which later I joined, explained to my superior that he has just had a son and that he was not able to carry out the tasks assigned to him in a more professional manner. He asked that he be replaced. The superior approved this but told him to find a colleague who would replace him. Since I, as well as other colleagues, were present at that meeting, this colleague of mine asked me to replace him, which I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having accepted your colleague's request, what was your immediate superior's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I, of course, asked him what the matter at hand was and how we were to go to work, how we would carry out our work. And my superior told me that, in addition to regular obligations, we would have to assist our colleagues in that working group in collecting materials and documents; that I would be given more concrete information there; that this was temporary; and while assistance was needed, I would be working there, too.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, at that time, did you know that some other colleagues of yours also offered different types of assistance to the working group for documenting war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I believe that the next day, when I went to the offices of the SVR Skopje in the crime unit, I saw other colleagues from police stations, among which was Canka Meglenova, a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have just told us, since your engagement was temporary, can you tell us how long did your engagement last upon your superior's order?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I believe from the middle of September until -- I can't recall precisely, but I remember that in October I was appointed as part of the working group. So it would be until the middle of December [as interpreted], approximately one month.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that later on you were appointed as a fully fledged member of the working group. But while you were still temporarily assigned in providing assistance to the working group, did you learn about the nature of that working group and when it had been established?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: During the first days when we met, there were also other colleagues there. We were interested, of course, to know what our tasks would be. Zoran Pavlovski was among the others present, who was then senior inspector at the homicide unit, and Tomislav [as interpreted] Stojanovski. He explained there was a working group established somewhere or sometime in May, that there were other colleagues who were permanent members of that group, and that they would give us concrete tasks. They would tell us the assistance we would need to provide them in the course of our work there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to how long had the group existed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I believe I already said that it was set up in the course of May 2001. I came in September 2001.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you, Mr. Stojkov, to look at the document which is after tab 1 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit number 1D115. The Macedonian page is 1D4328; whereas, the English page is 1D4330.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, did you ever see this document before?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I have not seen this document, but this is probably the document which, in the month of May, establishes this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the second page of this document together, which is 1D4331 in English and 1D4329 in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under bullet point 2, you can see the description of the goals or the tasks of this working group. According to this description, the working group is tasked with gathering evidence on military crimes committed on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. Would this description reflect the information that you received from your colleagues when you joined the working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. On that first working meeting, we were told that the members of the working group should be assisted in the area of gathering documents and documenting events connected with -- events reported as committed – I mean as war crimes that occurred after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, you have just told us that having been tasked with the duties, it went to Skopje, to the sector for the internal affairs of the Ministry of Interior. What was there?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: The place where we went, this was the homicide unit. This was where our first working meeting was with the other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, at that place, at the Skopje sector of internal affairs, did the working group continue working there, or did you have an office elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: When I started working first as assistant and then as a member of this working group, we used the offices from the unit of homicide; that is to say, the office of Mr. Zoran Pavlovski.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under bullet point 3 -- or rather, bullet point 2, paragraph 26 the decision from the month of May, it says that the working group will be would be stationed in Kumanovo. Did you know when and why had been transferred to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Later on, when I was appointed as member of this working group, and even before that, I could see that in the unit for internal affairs Kumanovo, some documents are coming to us, some cases, Official Notes, official documents were coming to us. And I know that in SVR Kumanovo, one of the inspectors still was working as a member of the working group, even though a lot of documents came there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, please, could you now look at the document after tab 2, which is exhibit number 1D116.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Macedonian page number is 1D4324, and the English page number is 1D4326.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left corner of this document, you will see that the document was issued by the Ministry of Interior on the 9th of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will see that the document was signed by Mr. Ljube Boskoski, Minister of the Interior. Tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. This is decision appointing me and my colleague, Canka Meglenova, as permanent members of this working group.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What does it imply for the permanent members of the group? What's the meaning of that, being a permanent member?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: This means, since we were both operative employees, that we take the operative work necessary to collect, gather the materials from police stations, from police bodies, where a possible act related to war crimes have been called in.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, when you were telling us about your superior in Gazi Baba, telling you that you would be assisting the working group, you said that at the time you were engaged on other tasks. Mr. Stojkov, from the moment you were appointed a permanent member of the working group, what was your main task or assignment?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: My main task was once an application was received that a war crime might have been committed, that a crime might have been committed related to war crimes, then we would carry out investigation whether such an act has been committed; and if so, to document the same event.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could be explain to the Court on the basis of what you, the working group, and you yourself operated?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: When I arrived, first as inspector assisting the members of the working group and later as its member, we received material containing a chronological overview with dates and days, events that were called in by injured parties and citizens or by other relatives or friends if the case had been of kidnapped individuals or deceased individuals.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain where did the injured parties or their families and friends report those cases or these events that concerned them and you would then assess whether they constituted crimes.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As a rule, not only the crimes that we worked on, which were suspected of being part of war crimes, but all crimes and all injured parties in the country on any which basis, first has to call in this event in the responsible police station or at the Ministry of Interior with the inspectors. On rare occasions, it happens that this is reported to a different police station or a different municipality if the person reporting this crime is from another town.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that those reports were filed by the injured parties off their relatives at the police station or at the department of internal affairs, tell me, please, to what extent that you, as members of the working group, relied on those bodies that were receiving the criminal reports from the injured parties?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: These are police stations or units for internal affairs which are bound by law. When someone feels injured or wishes to report a crime, they're bound by law to undertake measures. If it's the injured party, it is necessary they have to carry out an interview. They have to register a report of this kind has been submitted. Whether this be done by the person or their relatives, it is their obligation by law to document this.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So my question was, and if I understood you well, you stated that, of course, you did rely upon those bodies. Is this how I can understand what you just clarified?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the sector for internal affairs, Skopje, where your office was located, were there also bodies that rendered assistance to your working group, or were there individuals in those bodies who had the duty to render certain assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In the sector for internal affairs, Skopje, of course we could not carry out all tasks by ourselves. Most often and most assistance was given to us by the homicide unit; and since we were in the office of Mr. Zoran Pavlovski, who was a senior homicide inspector at the time, most frequently and most often we were assisted by him. Also, each time we went on the site of event, if there was need of police officers of inspectors from the police station or of the unit where we were working, if we needed help, we requested it. But most often, we resorted to the people from the homicide unit and the people from criminalistics, forensic unit.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering the tasks you performed there and the issues regarding which you had the duty to collect evidence, was the assistance rendered by those departments for homicides and the police forensics, was it more important than the assistance that any other bodies within the ministry would render?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: No. Most assistance came from the homicide unit and, as I said, from the forensic unit. Without their assistance -- they came with us if we needed to document an event, if we needed to document an event, photo documentation, forensic biological evidence, something which we're -- something that I and my colleagues from the group were not skilled to do. We are not skilled to do such forensics. I recall, when I came to the working group, we were working on a case of a three-year-old girl being shot in the back, in the spine. Her father was shot in the left side of the head and the shoulder, with shrapnel. Their vehicle was, in fact, attacked, I believe, near the village of Brvenica near Tetovo. When we received written information of this event having occurred and that the girl and father are in hospital, we asked for our colleagues from the forensic unit and from the homicide unit, Mr. Zoran Pavlovski. We first went to the hospital where our colleagues from forensics did their job. I know that they received from the doctors the bullet that was taken from the wounded girl and the pieces of shrapnel from the father. The next day my colleagues from forensics carried out a ballistic and other examination of the vehicle, which means that without them -- they conducted the on-site investigation. Without them and their work, we could not have information about this event.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojkov, you stated and repeated that you worked in the working group on the basis of reports by the inured parties, their families, or friends. Tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, whether the national affiliations, ethnic affiliations of the victim had any impact on any operation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Surely not. Professionalism, in the way of work, for us it was not important whether the case was reported -- the reported case was about a Macedonian, Albanian, Turk, or other. We had cases of injured parties, regardless of -- of it be physical injuries or murder or there was a property damage, their house had been burned down, and so forth. It was not important to us that the ethnic affiliation, the ethnicity of the injured party was.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now, Mr. Stojkov, to explain your manner of work in a way. When you would learn in any way on the basis of lists of reports that you had reports coming from injured parties of -- or if you learned in a different way that some injured party or a relative had reported an event, what would do you then? Could you explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Form the time when I joined the working group, I said that we received an overview of events that have happened, where there is suspicion of an act being committed related to war crimes. This overview is compiled on the basis of reports of injured parties or their families. This was done in a chronological basis with various data. There were some incomplete information; only the name and the place where the person came from. Sometime there is was no last name, no date of birth. There were other cases of complete information also. On the daily working meetings that we had, we would agree that we would start working on a particular case, about a particular person or event, and we -- our starting point was the police station from where the report originated.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if the police station was your first contact point or the place where the report was filed, what would you do there? What would you try to learn there?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: At the police station, there were -- there are all initial documents about a certain event or an injured party. If the person was received by a police officer, inspector, or duty officer, the latter were obliged to carry out an interview with that person. In the case of kidnap persons, his family came -- come to report this, and the officers have to take basic information in this regard; how long the person has been missing, how do they know that this person is kidnapped, do they suspect that the person is being kidnapped. These are basic Official Notes related to reports such as these, basic information about the person who is reporting the crime, friends, family. Our initial data base started from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since there were several of you in the group, when you would go to a police station, how would you proceed? Would you go on an individual basis or was there any other way in which you organised your visits to police stations or to the location within the ministry where the crime was reported?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: When we worked on the territory of the city of Skopje, most often my colleague and I -- my colleague, Canka Meglenova, and I, or I together with Zoran Pavlovski. In cases where we needed homicide assistance, sometimes all three of us went. If this was a bigger case that included more than one person or cases that required the presence of all three of us, in the cases outside of Skopje, most often in Tetovo area, I went with Apostol Stojanovski, who was then main inspector in the homicide unit in the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you would gather those basic information from the police station and the information that they probably had obtained performing their duties as prescribed by the law, what would be the further course, the further task of your working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Once we would receive the basic information, we would collect all official documents. We were the ones that collected them. We made copies of all existing document, which we thought we would need at that moment. The second part of our group consisted with contact with police forensics, because in concrete cases there were records of photographs of on-site inspections. And if there was material of this kind, we received this material from them. We collected this material, and I opened up files for most of such cases, files in which I put all materials that we collected. We open a file. Official Notes and other written materials are put in there; photo documentation or records from on-site inspections from police forensics.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As members of the working group, did you try or was it within your sphere of competence to have an interview with the injured party, if the injured party was living of course and available, and with other individuals who would know something about the injured party and the family thereof?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I already said, that's the third part of the work we did; the first being gathering information from police stations and internal affairs units, then work with police forensics. The third part of our work was in the case of finding the injured party, be it a kidnapped person or a maltreated person. We're not taking about in this case about a killed person. If we establish contacts with the families of some of the deceased or with other persons who are aware of this case, this is what we would do: We go and find such people, conduct interviews with them. With some we are unable to do so because people did not want to talk to us, both in the cases of Macedonians and Albanians and others. This was still a period of traces of the military conflict, and many of the people were still afraid. They did not want to talk with us. We -- it was a matter of their own free will. If they wanted to, they would talk to us. Our job was to find them and to ask them to talk to us. If we did and if we received information from them, then we documented this, and this was kept a secret. We kept this under a complete secret because we did not want to compromise these people.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Stojkov, you stated that you organised case files on every individual or case. Where did you keep these case files, considering the degree of confidentiality that you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I said, there was a case file for each case. We entered all documents, photographs from the persons, other materials, all documents, photographs, everything that we had related to that case. These case files were kept in binders which were in a metal safe box located in our office. I should also mention that the materials were copied in -- two copies were made of these materials. This was the case with all materials. One should be sent to our analytic service, and then again, through that, to the public prosecutor's office. We kept the materials in our office, in a metal safe box in our office that was also locked.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, Mr,. Stojkov, during that at the time when you were working in the working group, how many cases roughly you processed or how many cases you had?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact figure, since after we would finish with a given number of cases, five, ten, or if they were interrelated, if they were about a group of kidnapped persons, persons who were kidnapped on the same date from the same place, we had a case file on every individual. So we collated those old case files; and accompanied by an Official Note, we sent them to the analytics department when they were further processed. So maybe we had someone hundred, 200 case files. I can't say precisely, because I know that some of the casings were not closed. The events were registered but we were unable to close those cases.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you something else. Was there a head or a coordinator who coordinated the work of the working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: There was no head. There was a coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was that while you were there?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, from the outset when I came from September and later in October when I became a permanent member, coordinator was Mr. Apostol Stojanovski, who was the chief inspector the homicide department in the MOI.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this working group work separately on separate cases or did you have common meetings at which you discussed your joint work?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Considering the work that -- of the group that operated in Skopje, which consisted of me, Mrs. Canka Meglenova, Mr. Zoran Pavlovski who spent a lot of time with us, and Mr. Apostol Stojanovski, we had meetings. Maybe not every day, but every other day or every third day, we had meetings to agree which cases we were processing, which cases were closed, which should be sent to the analytics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that the superiors in the ministry, did they want to know what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: The initial contacts between us from the working group with the others, with the analytics department and with our superior officers, went through Mr. Apostol Stojanovski. However, since beside being a part of the working group, he also worked on the department of homicide across the entire territory of Macedonia, very frequently I would stand in for him at some of the meetings which we had the director, Mr. Goran Mitevski.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Mitevski's attitude towards the work of your working group? Did he support you, did he encourage you, or did he let you do things the way you deemed fit?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I can speak about all the meetings that I attended, brief meetings, where the director wanted, demanded to see what we did, how far things went. I know that he was very interested in everything we did. We had contacts at least once a week over the telephone or one of us would go for a brief meeting with him, presenting some of the documents that were near completion. He told us that it was very important for the ministry to have all these cases registered, reported, fully documented. He also told us that we enjoyed the full support from the then Minister of Interior, that with regards to assistance from other service, equipment, police forensics, and everything; that if we needed anything, it would be made available to us; that we needed to perform our work with utmost professionalism.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkov. And now I would like to move on to another topic, and I would kindly ask you to tell me what you know about that topic. You have told you that you based your work on the reports of the aggrieved persons or the persons who were their family members or knew the aggrieved persons. When you joined the group, and after that, did you know whether anybody from the village of Ljuboten, as an aggrieved person, reported an incident or a circumstance, under which an alleged event might have taken place and under which he might have been an aggrieved person?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In the overview that we received, there were no reports speaking about aggrieved parties. I'm speaking about persons with bodily injuries or ill-treatment or the houses of home were burned down. There was no information that any police organ had received any such reports.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although in the overview of the reported filed by either aggrieved persons or on their behalf, you did not have a single person from the village of Ljuboten. Tell me, did the working group, however, at one point in time started working on the events in Ljuboten and around it?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I do not remember the period exactly, but I know that it was immediately after the under-secretary in the Ministry of Interior was dismissed. I know that there was a change of office, and Mr. Spasen Sofeski, I believe, came to work as under-secretary of the forensics police, of crime police. In a working meeting, Mr. Apostol Stojanovski came. We were in the office, we were working, and we were organizing some of the documents and case files. Mr. Apostol told us -- he spoke to me directly incidentally, and he told me: "Please open a new case file. We will need to deal with the Ljuboten event."

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the request of the coordinator of your group, did you react in any way?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I reacted personally regarding the entire situation. I told him that, in the overview, there was no report that there were injured parties related to Ljuboten case, and that this deviates from all the standard measures and activities that our working group was carrying out. This would be completely outside of the context of our operation. I don't remember precisely, but I believe Apostol said that this was an order, or maybe not order, a task given by our superiors and that we needed to process that case.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, in answering my questions, you have told us that you did not have any prejudices or any position as to whether you would be dealing with the aggrieved persons who were Macedonians, Albanians, or others. Now what has prompted this reaction of yours? Was it because the alleged victims were Albanians, or was it something else, something to the effect that you have just explained?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I live in the settlement Radisani, which is very close to the Ljuboten village, and I can tell that you I have very good friends there until the present day. I'm referring to my Albanian friends, so my ethnic affiliations does not have anything to do with this. For me, a case is a case, whether the aggrieved parties are Macedonians or Albanians. You know what? I was processing a case where an Albanian was an injured party in the village of Aracinovo. A senior citizen came to the police station Avtokomanda and reported that, in his house, there was a warehouse. He was involved in trade, and some of the merchandise was stolen. I believe it was car or tractor batteries and spare parts for tractors because that person had a shop. After the case was reported, we investigated. We were looking for information, and we found the perpetrators. The perpetrators were Macedonians. Those individuals were brought in. Their homes were searched. The stolen goods were found; and through the competent police station, a criminal report was filed, which was then forwarded to the competent public prosecutor's office, that later took its own course of action. So that I believe the division that some people, during that time possibly made, had no impact in our working group. It was not present there. For us, a case was a case. I can't make any distinction between an Albanian or a Macedonian child.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, tell me, please, after this reaction of yours and after had you seen that there were no reports by the aggrieved persons, what did your working group decide with regard to the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pavlovski made a suggestion that we establish a normal procedure from the following day onwards; to go visit the police stations in the area of which the Ljuboten case took place and where we should start processing it as in the other cases; to try and find some documents, materials; to see what happened; whether there were aggrieved persons; whether were there any reports; whether there was any damage caused. So on the next day, we started processing the Ljuboten case.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that for every new case, as you've told us, you put together a file, did something similar happen with this new task that you were given to investigate and what happened? Were there any aggrieved persons coming from Ljuboten and in relation to the events surrounding Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, immediately after we open a case file, we are opening a case file. I opened this case file. I wrote in my own hand "Ljuboten." Some of the files were typed on a computer; some were done on a typewriter. In the morning when we out, I just took a binder and I wrote there "Ljuboten" in my own hand. And we, with Mr. Pavlovski, took the official car and visited the police station Mirkovci. This is where we wanted to start our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If understand you properly, you said that you had visited the police station at which the incident had been reported or where the incident had happened. Why did you go to the Mirkovci station on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Mirkovci is an auxiliary station attached to the OVR Cair. OVR Cair consists of Cair police station, Mirkovci police station, and the department for operations, inspectorate, et cetera. I believe that we had some information that some persons from within that event were brought in into the Mirkovci police station, or they were brought to the Mirkovci police station. We decided to start from there; and, of course, our plan was to visit the Cair police station as well and all the other places that we needed to visit.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Mirkovci police station, who did you find there? Did you have any conversations at the police station in Mirkovci with anybody about the task which had brought you to the Mirkovci police station in the first place?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, in the police station, as I said already, Mr. Pavlovski and I went there with our official jeep, Lada, and we parked it in the yard of the police station. Several police officers wearing uniforms were in front of the station. Some of them were still wearing camouflage uniforms, and we went into the police station. And immediately when you go inside the station, on your right-hand side, there is an office which is the reception desk. The duty police officer is there. We introduced ourselves to the duty police officers as the rules require, and he introduced himself to us. I don't remember his name. I know that he is not of Macedonian ethnicity. And we told him that we wanted to discuss issues with the some of the superior officers from that police station, and he retorted that, at that moment, only the deputy commander of that police station was present there. We asked him to announce us, since we had some interview to carry out with him. The deputy commander received us as at his office. I can't remember the name or the family name. I know that it ended with I-C. I remember this because, again, it is not a Macedonian family name. It ended with I-C. I don't know. And the deputy commander was also wearing camouflage uniform. And after we went in, after we sat down, after we completed the preliminaries, the introduction, we explained the reason for our visit and what issues interested us.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, before you continue describing what happened at the police station, I have noticed that, on several occasions, you have emphasised that the policemen and the commander wore camouflage uniforms.
