Can you tell me, approximately, when it was when you were tasked with the Ljuboten case and when you went to the Mirkovci police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Of course, it was in 2002, but what period. I told you that I believe it was after the arrival of Mr. -- of the new under-secretary, Mr. Spasen Sofeski. It was during that period. I can't remember the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you notice that? Why was it important for you that the policemen and the deputy commander wore camouflage uniforms? What about other commanders at other police stations, for example, in Skopje? How did they come to work? Did they also wear camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, regarding other commanders, in the context that we had, I don't think they wore camouflage uniform. But the Mirkovci police station is -- first of all, it is competent for the part of territory gravitating towards Kosovo border. And during that period of time, there was still data coming that uniformed persons with weapons were observed, that some goods were transferred across the state border to Kosovo -- or from Kosovo, and that was -- there is a mountainous area. I believe there were still reasons, or maybe the colleagues were moving in that part towards the border and this is why they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're moving with a view to finishing this evening just a little after 6.30. So we'll adjourn now and resume at 5.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention that if you are feeling unwell, just indicate that to us, and we will take a measure to bring the proceedings to an end for the day. We understand you're not feeling entirely as well as you would like. We will keep this session short as much as we can. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were saying that when you arrived at the Mirkovci police station that you talked to a superior there. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you can remember, what did you talk about and what did he inform you of?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We talked to the deputy commander. We informed him the reasons why -- of the reasons why we were there, who we are, why we are here, that we are interested in all events regarding the Ljuboten events, and what happened concretely on that day and several days before and afterwards. The deputy explained to us that, on the day of the Ljuboten event, he was on site, that he was not in the police station, but that some of the police officers had been at the police stations at that time and could provide some more concrete information. We asked him whether there was official materials about some events on that day, whether something was in written form, and whether we could look at it; and if something was of interest to us, whether we could take it with us. The deputy explained - my apologies - that the overall material was transferred to analytics in Cair, which then transfers it to SVR in Cair, and that he doesn't believe that other than matters in the daily log-book, other materials would not be found. After we left the deputy, as I already said, we saw some police officers --

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Stojkov. Allow me to interrupt you. You said that the deputy commander was not at the police station on the day, but did you talk to him and did you learn from him whether he had any knowledge as to what was going on at the station, or maybe he did not learn subsequently about that, at all?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We asked him, as I said, and he said he was not in the police station; but whether it was that evening or the next day when he came, he saw that there were people brought in, and that a larger amount of weapons and ammunition was brought in. And this is why, in effect, we requested the documents to see who and what persons were brought in, what weapons were brought in, what has happened to these people, and this is why we requested the documents.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have interrupted you when you started talking about you coming to the station and seeing several policemen there. Did you and your colleague, Zoran, talk to these people; and if you did, what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We first asked -- we explained the time-period we were interested about. We saw him -- we saw them in the hallways of the police station, and we asked them whether in these days or on the day of the Ljuboten event was working -- whether he was in the police station or whether they were at the points that were covered by the police station Mirkovci. I remember that one of my -- one of the colleagues that day had been at one of the points, and one was a duty officer or a deputy duty officer. I believe Dragan was his name. He told me that on that day there were a lot of events. There was a lot of going on, that he documented all of this. There were Official Notes to that extent. We wanted to have a official interview with them; but, as I already said, all of our interviews or we took all of the statements on a voluntary basis only if the person would agree to speak with us, since we were not authorised to impose or instruct anyone to give us statements.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, when you received the information from the deputy commander, who told you that the documents were in Cair and from the policeman who told that you he had personally written numerous documents, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We agreed to go to the police station Cair the next day. However, the next day, my colleague, Pavlovski, was charged with other tasks, so I called my colleague, Canka Meglenova. And we agreed that after stopping at the police forensics first to get some material we needed to get from there, we would go visit the police station Cair.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you remember when you arrived at Cair, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact time, perhaps it was around 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Cair, did you talk to anyone, or let me put it this way: What happened when you arrived at the Cair police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Once we arrived, the standard procedure; we called, we entered the room of the officers on duty, we requested to meet with some of the superiors of the OVR Cair, whether the head or the commander of the police station. We were told that the head of OVR Cair was present, Mr. Ljube Krstevski, and that he would receive us.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did Mr. Krstevski receive you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: In his office. His secretary came out, she greeted us in the hallway, and took us to his office.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mr. Krstevski.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We introduced ours first; although, we had known each other from before. We told him that we were members of the working group and that we were interested in the events around Ljuboten; first whether there were reported aggrieved persons, and then we requested to see whether there were documents or notes from this event, prior to the event, or after the event.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what Mr. Krstevski told you? How did he respond?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We were very well received by him in his office; and half jokingly, he said that we should have been there that day to see the chaos that happened that day. Then we started talking more seriously about the event itself, the reasons for this event, and this whole situation. Mr. Krstevski said that this whole event was preceded by a mine explosion of a military vehicle with soldiers being killed; then how local inhabitants of the village of Ljubanci and others that gravitate around the village of Ljuboten were upset because soldiers from the army of the Republic of Macedonia were killed that came from Ljubanci; that movement was noted of uniformed persons with weapons in black uniforms with emblems of the NLA in the region above the village of Ljuboten, in the village itself; and that on that day, on the day of the event itself, there were major problems with the population from the Macedonian villages and from people from the settlements that came that day. He also said that there were a lot of people that were brought there and detained in police station Cair and Mirkovci, and also that a lot of weapons were also found.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, how long did you talk to Mr. Krstevski? Did he provide you with all the details, or did he just choose and pick some of the details that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Our conversation lasted about half an hour to 40 minutes. This was a conversation in fragments. We skipped from one topic to another about how things happened. Then we talked about the events after the event itself; what happened to the persons that were brought in, whether and where they were transferred or took over from other police stations, from the prosecutor from the courts that reports were written and prepared. At this time, this segments did not mean much to us; later how they attempted to enter the village and that allegedly there were people killed. But all of this was done in segments. We requested that we be allowed -- first, we asked if there was written documents on this matter, and Ljube said that all events were registered and that there is a document for each event, after which we requested to see these documents. And we explained that, if necessary, we would ask him to secure or to allow us to take copies with us.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, in light of the fact that you arrived there to look at the documentation, as you've told us, did Mr. Krstevski allow to you do that and where did that -- did that take place, if it was ever allowed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Even as the conversation was ongoing, Krstevski called one of the people responsible in the analysis unit in Cair. We were told that we were free to go there and to look at any materials we may deem necessary, to make copies of them, and to take them with us, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, did you ask only for the documents describing the events in the village, or did you also ask for documents describing events outside the village at police check-points? How broad was the scope of your interest at the moment when you spoke to Mr. Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: There were some rumours in the public that, allegedly, the small number of police officers, who were there in that region at that time in the roads around Ljuboten, that they maltreated people at check-points, that they beat them up, they physically harassed them. This was one of the points that we were working on, and this is why we asked whether something like this had happened, that that there was a complaint or a statement, whether someone had requested to clarify a situation of this kind with the police officers. The head responded that up until then, nobody had requested, nobody had reported of any grievances, nor had anyone submitted a complaint about the police officers or their behaviour. There was no such report from the citizens or the villagers of Ljuboten to the official police services.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, when you spoke to Mr. Krstevski, did he ever tell you whether you were the first who had shown interest in the event or whether there were people who had come before from the Ministry of Interior, the courts, the prosecutor's offices, to ask for similar information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We didn't catch any of that on the transcript, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm just saying I do apologise for the interruption, but I feel that this is quite an important issue here, and the question does appear to be quite leading. I would ask that it be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A little late now, Mr. Dobbyn, yes. But I'm sure Ms. Residovic will take care in future.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, and I will certainly make sure that my questions to the witness are not leading.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- or let me put it this way: During the course of your fragmentary conversation, as you put it, with the head of the police station, did you also discuss any other acts on behalf of other people with regard to these events?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: If you mean police procedures regarding the people who were brought in and detained, we talked about the fact that they were listed and recorded in police documents. Those who requested medical attention received medical attention. Those that needed expertise to be conducted, papillary lines were taken. Traces were found from use of weapons, the paraffin glove. All of this was reported to the responsible bodies, the duty centre, the public prosecutor's office, investigating judge, and that criminal reports were issued against some persons, if this is what you had in mind when you said "procedures."

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go back to the same question maybe a little later. For the time being, I would like to thank you for the explanation provided thus far. Now, tell me, did you finally get hold of the documents that had brought you to the OVR Cair in the first place?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: After Mr. Krstevski called his colleagues at analytic unit, we stayed a little while longer in his office because we knew that there were people -- that there were dead bodies in the village. We knew that on the next day, or on the 14th, attempts were made to make an organised entry into the village of Ljuboten in order to carry an on-site investigation and forensic investigation that would allow the prosecutors and investigating judges to see the site. I know that contacts were made with a Member of Parliament of Albanian ethnicity, Fatmir Etemi. Through the media, we already had some information about all of this. So we asked Mr. Krstevski, in light of the fact that he was also included in these events and these activities, what and how had been done in this respect. He told us and he explained in short that two attempts were made to enter the village, that contacts were made with Mr. Etemi, that the security situation did not allow entry into the village, and that forensic teams, medical teams, judges, prosecutors were on standby and were ready to enter but that they did not do so.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, my question may not have been exactly precise. What you have just told us now is something that you already told us before. What I would like to know is this: When you finished talking to Mr. Krstevski 30 or 45 minutes later, did Mr. Krstevski allow you to enter the analytics department?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. We were allowed to do that and we went there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were you looking for there? Did you have a period in mind, or did you have a random look at all the documents?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Of course, we told our colleagues who were working there that we needed the documents from the period around August 2001; but, as a rule, we first asked to see the book with Official Notes and the book with operations information, in order to find there the numbers, and on the basis of the identifying elements to find the case files that we were looking for, and then take them out. So we did not need to take all the case files from that sector, and this was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you receive the operations book and the Official Notes book that you asked for; and if you received them, did you find anything in them?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: The books were given to us to inspect them; but in reviewing them, I could not find what I was interested in at the moment and neither could my colleague. So we asked to see all written documents from that period.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was given to you? What did the documents consist of, the ones that you inspected?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We asked to see all telegrams, information documents, Official Notes from the period few days before the Ljuboten event and maybe a week later than the Ljuboten event.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the form of all these documents? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I said, those were telegrams, information notes, and the Official Notes. They were placed in binders, and we found them. Our colleagues, actually, from the analytics helped us. They gave us the binders. We sat down with my colleague and we were turning pages, reading the documents one by one. And with regard to documents that we considered useful for our work, we would mark those. And after we marked those documents that we felt we would need - I apologise - we asked that they are copied for us, that copies of those are made for us.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your colleagues make copies of the documents that you marked for copying?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. All documents that we marked were copied, the documents we marked, the documents that we felt we would need.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you had already spoken to people at the Mirkovci police station and since you had already spoken to Mr. Krstevski, when you were inspecting the documents in the analytics department, could you find any documents that would corroborate the words of the previous interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: From both conversations, the one in the Mirkovci police station, the conversation with my colleagues there, and also the conversation with Mr. Krstevski, the information that we received orally were then found in the written materials. There were Official Notes, telegrams, information notes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to having spoken to Mr. Krstevski and having inspected documents at the analytics department, did you have any other conversations with anybody else at the OVR Cair?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We encountered some of the police officers at Cair as well. I don't remember, maybe they were inspectors, and we asked to see whether some of them were among the ones who participated or were deployed at Ljuboten during those days. We had conversations, but none of them wanted to give an official statement, you understand, and I was not authorised to order them, that they need to have interview with me. But during the unofficial conversations, I know that they told me that on that day, in front of the Cair police station, there were several hundreds of people gathered who protested, who wanted to go towards the part of Ljuboten village through Radisani; and that the colleagues, who were not many at that time there, had a great deal of problems, because the population of Macedonian ethnicity from the village of Radisani and lower from Radisani, in the part towards Butel settlement, in a way, apprehended the people from Ljuboten village, attacked them, were beating them. So the police officers needed really to recapture those people, to take them literally from their hands, to prevent any greater harm, and those people were taken to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, you've told us that you had arrived with a task to learn something about the allegedly aggrieved persons as a result of these incidents. Did you ever speak to Mr. Krstevski or anybody else, whether they, within the purview of their legal competencies, had they had any contacts with the possibly aggrieved from the village or elsewhere that might have some explanation for them?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I know that they had contacts with people from the villages; however, they had nothing specific. Nobody was willing to report any specific case. They knew -- I mean, they learned that there were dead people and that they were buried. They made attempts to contact people from the village, village inhabitants. However, everybody refused to have any cooperation, since they were fearing something and they were reluctant to cooperate with the police.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, what you have just related to us, the story of Mr. Krstevski and a number of your colleagues, about people attacking villagers and the police trying to save them, did you find all that plausible, the stories that your colleagues shared with you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Of course, I did believe the stories, primarily because they are my colleagues. They are authorised officers; and pursuant to the law, they need to safeguard the law and order. And, secondly, I personally had the opportunity to see what took place in front of the Cair police station on that date, and in the area around village of Radisani. So I personally saw some things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see that something was happening around the police station and Radisan village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, on the Sunday, 12th of August, 2001, I was working on the territory of my police station, Gazi Baba, and my task was to secure the facilities of vital importance on the territory of Gazi Baba police station, together with my colleagues. Around noon, through my radio station, well, there were allegations or rumours before that also; but around noon, I heard that something was taking place near village of Radisani. Because I live in the Radisani settlement, that is not far from the Radisani village and this is where my family live, I immediately went home.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you went home from Gazi Baba, how could you know what was happening in front of the Cair police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: The only road towards the Radisani settlement and the village of Radisani, as well as the villages of Ljubanci, Ljuboten, and other settlements and villages gravitating towards this area, passes by the Cair police station. On that date, when I started towards my home since I was fearing for my family, of course, and when I came in front of the Cair police station, I can't give you the exact time. It was 12.00 noon or 1.00 p.m. or early, I can't remember, and there were several hundred of people outside. They were shouting, they were protesting, and they were demanding something. They had Macedonian flags; that I remember. Also, there was a huge convoy of cars moving towards the village of Radisani and the Radisani settlement, and I saw all this and I was in a hurry to get home.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, you are a policeman. Did you stop even for a moment; and if you didn't, why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I did not stop in front of the police station, since I think that there were police officers inside the station who were able -- well, I saw several police officers who would most probably be deployed. I don't know whether they kept people at a distance. But, sincerely, I was concerned about my family because I didn't know what was taking place. So I was in a hurry to get home, since my children were then very young.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you leave your house to go somewhere? Did you see anything else in addition to what you saw on the way home?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: When I reached my home, I saw that my family was very agitated, and I believe that I needed to stay with them. However, from the upper floor of my house, from the upper balcony, you can see a section of the road towards Ljuboten and the upper part of the Radisani village. And at one point in time, I noticed a larger group of people moving towards the village of Ljuboten, towards the village of Radisani. Maybe there were cars there, too, but the location of the road is such that I saw people moving. I was not able to see cars. And from the lower part of village of Radisani, I saw another group of citizens, larger group of citizens, moving towards -- moving from the village towards the road, Ljubotenski Pat. And, suddenly, that group moving from Ljuboten, I suppose those were the Ljuboten inhabitants, suddenly they moved down across the fields, across the land there, to the village of Radisani.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I understand you well, you have given us one of the reasons why you trusted your colleagues who had told you that the civilians had attacked the villagers. Is that what you were saying when you were sharing with us your personal views of the day?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Well, since I stayed at home on that day with my family, the next day I went to work again, of course, but I had sometime to meet some of my colleagues who told me that there were situations. I later read about those in the documents, that there were situations that citizens of Macedonian ethnicity were stopping and attacking people of Albanian ethnicity from the village of Ljuboten and that police officers needed to intervene to save those people. So, of course, I trusted them, because I saw that happening with my own eyes. From both sides, a larger group of people were coming, people coming down from Ljuboten to the village of Radisani and also people from Butel moving towards the village of Radisani and the settlement of Radisani.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, again, for your explanation. Now let's go back to what you did as a member of the working group, and especially to what you and your colleague, Canka, saw on that day, what you chose and copied in the analytics department of the OVR Cair. Could we please look at some documents together. I will kindly ask you to tell me whether you can remember if you saw some of the documents before or whether you even copied some of them on the day at the OVR Cair. Could you please look at the document which is after tab 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P396.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, tell me, did you know who Slavko Ivanovski was?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't know. I didn't know who was the commander, I didn't know who was the deputy commander of Mirkovci police station. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the telegram. If I understood you well, among the documents at the analytics department, you also saw telegrams, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I also saw telegrams and I know the text of these telegrams. This is an official vehicle of the ARM where the soldiers were killed. I know the text of this. I don't think we took telegrams as part -- as documents in our case file, but I'm aware of this text. I know this text, which means that I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the document after tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exhibit P158.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is an Official Note of the Mirkovci police station, and its number is 1179.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: This is the same text of the telegram. There is a possibility that we took this document with us because it is an Official Note. It is the text dealing with the ARM vehicle when eight Macedonian soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue looking at documents together, when you spoke to Mr. Krstevski, did you ever talk about the action that took place on the 12th of August in his area of responsibility? Did you ever mention that? Did he make any references to that? Did you show any interest at all in learning about that action?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: No. As I said, this was a fragmented conversation. We skipped from one topic to another, but we began our conversation with the situation of the death of the eight Macedonian soldiers. I think that, in our discussions, we were told that military action has been taken, because we had a case of dead soldiers. Later, I also saw that the military positions were attacked by uniformed persons in the area of Ljuboten, as well as the police check-points, of course; if this was the extent of your question.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please look at the document after tab 5. This is another telegram by the Mirkovci police station. Can you recall having seen a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I already said, we did not take telegrams with us. They have different significance or different weight in our documents, but I know this text, and I know of it. If there is a telegram, surely, in the documents, there is also an Official Note to that extent. If there is such an Official Note, then we took it with us, but the text is known to me.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at the document after tab 6, which is Exhibit P150. As you've just told us, you also looked at the Official Notes. Do you remember having seen or copied this Note?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: As I said, since I know the text, I know of this. But whether we took all of the documents with us or whether we left this one, I cannot really respond, because I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please look at the document after tab 7, which is Exhibit 1D145. Although you told us already that you did not take any telegrams, if you look at the contents of this particular one, does this jog your memory as to what it contains?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I cannot recall now. There are some concrete information about those Zendelovksi family. I know that I had read material that prior to the Ljuboten event, there was movement of uniformed and armed persons. I believe I mentioned this earlier. Perhaps I had seen it; perhaps I had not seep it, this telegram. I know that we saw materials informing of movement of uniformed persons with weapons in the area of the village of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now look at the document after tab 8, which is Exhibit P151.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: This is an Official Note based on the telegram that was submitted. It is the same text in question. Most probably, it is possible that we made a copy of this and took it with us. This is an Official Note from police station Mirkovci.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, please, this is an Official Note, and we've seen others as well. Tell me, please, who is it normally who drafts an Official Note of this kind?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: We have the name and last name of the person who did so. Official Notes are prepared by all authorised officials depending on the activities undertaken: Duty officer, police officer, deputy duty officer. According to the name which can I see here, I'm thinking whether this is the person who was on duty when we were in police station Mirkovci. I cannot be certain of this; however, it is possible that this is that very person. However, I cannot say with certainty. Official Notes are otherwise prepared or drafted by the police officer all the way up to superiors and heads of certain units and services. All of them draft Official Notes about various activities and events.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document after tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P114.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the reports --.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I don't think we have the report on the screen yet. Could you please hold on just for a moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: This is a report about events registered and measures undertaken. I know that, during my visit to the analytics unit, I saw several reports. I know with certainty that I took them with me. I made copies of them, and I took them with me because these reports provide a chronological overview of the events and participants therein. This is why I can say with certainty that I took these documents with me.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's go to the document after tab 10, which is an Official Note dated 11 August 2001; again, issued by the police station of Mirkovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P159.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you had any recollection with regard to the document that is just before you.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: I can't remember this document concretely, but I know I said earlier that the army positions were attacked. Most probably, the army had also acted or responded to these attacks. Here, in the text, it is stated that ARM acted with infantry weapons in the direction of the village of Ljubanci, and this is information provided by a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let look at the document after tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P23, under seal. This is Official Note number 1131.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, do you remember having seen or having noticed or even having copied the Official Notes with similar contents or maybe even this particular one.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: This Official Note is known to me in principle. In all cases where we encountered Official Notes with persons, identity of persons and any other additional information about these persons were taken by us. This is a characteristic one because we have here listed and confiscated weapons, and these are the persons who were brought into the police station Mirkovci along with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why would these people be of any interest to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV
utterances.text: Once the event was over, we, as a working group, were charged to work on this. The understanding was that we were to find these persons, contact these persons, and to see, if possible, to establish contact with them, to see whether they can report or say something to us about their grievances. On the other hand, I remember that part of them were brought in with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MRS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will adjourn now for the day and we resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of February, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.34 p.m.,
